\title{A stabilizer-rank residual backend for \texttt{clifft}:\\
       an honest assessment on magic-sparse circuits}
\author{Research note (revised)}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\texttt{clifft} simulates Clifford$+T$ circuits with a symbolic Clifford frame
plus a dense $2^k$ active block. We build and validate a low-rank stabilizer
(CH-form) backend for the magic-sparse regime: minimal-extent $\{I,S\}$ magic
decomposition ($2^{0.228t}$), single-shot tensor-product magic sampling, BGH
norm estimation, and a global Clifford-frame composition, each checked against
a dense oracle and against \texttt{clifft} to machine precision. This revision
replaces the earlier draft's headline claim, which an adversarial review
refuted: the ``crossover at $n\!\approx\!22$'' was measured against
\texttt{clifft}'s \emph{unitary} path (peak rank $n$), while \texttt{clifft}'s
own \texttt{record\_probabilities} answers the same queries \emph{exactly} from
the measured program --- at peak rank $1$ on that benchmark's chain-IQP family
($\sim\!10^5\times$ faster than the number we charged it), and at peak rank
$n/2$ on dense random IQP. Re-benchmarked fairly (dense IQP, exact
$2^{n/2}$ baseline, exact meet-in-the-middle ground truth, and an error metric
that charges the \emph{full} pipeline), the true picture is: \texttt{clifft}'s
exact fast path wins to $n\!\approx\!34$; the backend overtakes at
$n\!\approx\!34$ for $\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.17$ and at $n\!\approx\!48$ for
$\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.08$, with a clean measured accuracy dial
$\mathrm{TV}=(0.50\pm0.01)\,\delta$; and beyond $n\!\approx\!62$ --- where every
exact method (dense block, forced replay, meet-in-the-middle) needs
$\gtrsim\!16$\,GB--$1$\,TB --- the backend is the only method that runs
($n{=}72$: $267$\,s, $1.9$\,GB, extrapolated $\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.18$). The
composition's ``free Clifford'' advantage is real but is
constant/poly-factor engineering with substantial prior art; we position it
accordingly.
\end{abstract}

\section{Motivation}
\texttt{clifft}'s state is split into (i) a \emph{symbolic Clifford frame}
evolving dormant axes for free, and (ii) a \emph{dense active block}, a $2^k$
statevector expanded only for non-Clifford content. A static profiler
(\texttt{research/stabrank\_profiling}) established two facts that scope this
work: $k$ is built from magic (plain Clifford superposition never inflates it),
and \texttt{clifft}'s measurement-reordering passes already shrink $k$
aggressively. The bet: when the active block is \emph{magic-sparse}, its
stabilizer rank is $\ll 2^k$ and a low-rank residual extends \texttt{clifft}'s
reach --- at the cost of exactness.

\section{Background and related work}
\paragraph{CH-form and low-rank decompositions.}
A stabilizer state is stored as $\ket{\phi}=\omega\,U_C U_H \ket{s}$
(Bravyi--Browne--Calpin--Campbell--Gosset--Howard~\cite{bravyi2019}): $O(n^2)$
bits per term, $O(n)$ Clifford gates, $O(n^2)$ Hadamard and single-amplitude
queries. A magic state is a sum $\ket\psi=\sum_a c_a\ket{\phi_a}$ of $\chi$
terms; Cliffords preserve $\chi$, each $T$ doubles it, measurement can collapse
it.

\paragraph{Related work (what is and is not new here).}
None of the individual ingredients is novel, and we position the composition
against its prior art explicitly. ``Cliffords paid once, exponential cost only
on the magic'' is the architecture of Bravyi--Gosset~\cite{bravyi2016} already;
Qassim, Wallman and Gosset~\cite{qassim2019} recompile circuits into
non-Clifford rotations times a single global Clifford precisely to speed up
CH-form simulators; Garc\'ia--Markov~\cite{garcia2015} shared a stabilizer
frame across superposition terms a decade ago; Pauli-based
computation~\cite{peres2023} absorbs all Cliffords into adaptive Pauli
measurements on $t$ magic qubits. The closest single work is Pashayan et
al.~\cite{pashayan2022}: gadgetize the $T$'s, then \emph{statically} compress
the global Clifford and the outcome projector into an effective magic register
before running a stabilizer-rank estimator. Stabilizer tensor networks with
magic injection~\cite{nakhl2025} pair a Clifford frame with an MPS residual;
\texttt{quizx}~\cite{kissinger2022} reaches the same ``decompose only the
magic'' endpoint via ZX rewriting. What this prototype adds is the
\emph{online} form of the composition: a persistent global frame maintained
gate-by-gate over a CH-form term sum, with \texttt{clifft}-style
measurement-driven active-subspace collapse, supporting mid-circuit and
adaptive measurement --- plus the engineering observation (verified in
qiskit-aer's source) that the flagship open-source CH-form simulator,
\texttt{extended\_stabilizer}, applies every Clifford per-term at $O(\chi)$
cost, with no frame. The advantage is a constant/poly factor, never an
exponent, and we claim nothing more for it.

\section{Method}

\subsection{Minimal-extent magic decomposition (the $0.228$ exponent)}
$T = \alpha I + \beta S$ with
$\alpha=\tfrac12+i\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}{2}$, $\beta=\bar\alpha$, both terms
Clifford, $|\alpha|+|\beta| = 2^{0.114}$, so the stabilizer extent per $T$ is
$2^{0.228}$ --- optimal within the extent framework, since extent is
multiplicative for tensor products of single-qubit states~\cite{bravyi2019}.
Branching in the computational basis instead costs extent $2^t$, which
sparsification cannot repair; this basis choice is the crux.

\subsection{Sparsification and single-shot magic sampling}
Importance-sampling $k$ terms from $p_a=|c_a|/\lVert c\rVert_1$ gives an
unbiased $\ket\omega$ with
$\mathbb{E}\lVert\ket\psi-\ket\omega\rVert^2=(\lVert c\rVert_1^2-\lVert\psi\rVert^2)/k$;
$k\sim 2^{0.228t}/\delta^2$ bounds the 2-norm error by $\delta$. For
\emph{product} magic (IQP's $\ket T^{\otimes n}$) the branch strings factorize
and we sample them directly --- unbiased, no $2^t$ built, and no factor-$t$
variance accumulation (streaming mid-circuit sparsification pays that factor;
it remains implemented but is not the benchmarked path).

\subsection{Norm estimation and normalization}\label{sec:norm}
$P(x)=|\bra x\psi\rangle|^2/\lVert\psi\rVert^2$ needs $\lVert\psi\rVert^2$
without materializing $2^n$; we implement the BGH estimator (Lemmas 2--4,
$O(n^3)$ exponential sum, validated exactly). Two honesty points the earlier
draft blurred. (i) The estimator's per-sample relative spread is $\approx\!1.2$,
so $L$ samples give $\approx\!1.2/\sqrt L$ relative error \emph{on every
reported probability}; at the $L=30$--$80$ used previously that is an
$11$--$22\%$ multiplicative error, the same order as the sparsification error
--- and the old ``norm-free TV'' metric cancelled it exactly. (ii) For the
benchmark family --- \emph{unitary} product-magic circuits ---
$\lVert\psi\rVert=1$ exactly and
$\mathbb{E}\lVert\omega\rVert^2 = 1+(\lVert c\rVert_1^2-1)/k$ is known
analytically, so normalization needs no estimation at all
(\texttt{samples=0} mode). We benchmark with analytic normalization and report
the estimated-norm mode separately; \emph{generic} circuits (projections,
non-product magic) must pay the estimator, whose cost to keep the norm error
subdominant scales as $\chi L \sim 2^{0.228t}/\delta^4$ --- a real limitation,
stated as such.

\subsection{Error guarantee, stated precisely}\label{sec:guarantee}
Sparsification bounds the \emph{2-norm} error
$\lVert\psi-\omega\rVert\le\delta$. For a single target that yields an
\emph{additive} amplitude error of typical size $\delta\,2^{-n/2}$ --- i.e.\ a
$\sim\!\delta$ \emph{relative} error on \emph{typical} (anticoncentrated) IQP
probabilities $P(x)\sim2^{-n}$, which is what the measured
$\mathrm{TV}\approx0.5\,\delta$ reflects. It is \textbf{not} a per-$x$
relative-error guarantee: individual small probabilities can be off by more.
Guaranteed relative error costs the exact-rank methods
($2^{0.396t}$~\cite{qassim2021}).

\subsection{Clifford-frame composition}
As in the earlier draft: $\ket{\mathrm{state}}=F(\sum_a\ket{\phi_a})$ with $F$
a global Clifford updated in $O(n)$ per gate; magic and measurement act on the
terms conjugated through $F$ at the optimal $\{I,S\}$ extent. Validated
against the plain engine (including forced-outcome measurement) to
$6\times10^{-15}$.

\section{The honest baseline}\label{sec:baseline}
The earlier draft timed \texttt{clifft.basis\_probabilities} on the
\emph{unitary} IQP program, forcing $\mathrm{peak\_rank}=n$. That is not how a
user computes $P(x)$: compiling the \emph{measured} program and calling
\texttt{record\_probabilities} (exact forced replay) exploits
\texttt{clifft}'s measurement-driven reduction. Measured facts
(\texttt{validate\_mitm.py}, review session):
\begin{itemize}
\item On the old benchmark's nearest-neighbour-CZ IQP the measured program
compiles to $\mathrm{peak\_rank}=1$ (lightcone sweep):
\texttt{record\_probabilities} returns the same $96$ exact probabilities in
$0.2$\,ms at $n{=}26$ --- vs the $23$\,s the old benchmark charged
\texttt{clifft} and the $1.3$\,s our backend took. \textbf{The old crossover
was an artifact of the baseline.}
\item On \emph{dense} random IQP (CZ on each pair w.p.\ $\tfrac12$, the
standard hard ensemble) the measured program compiles to
$\mathrm{peak\_rank}=n/2$: the honest exact baseline is $2^{n/2}$, not $2^n$.
\item Independently, a meet-in-the-middle (MitM) evaluator
(\texttt{chform\_cpp/mitm\_iqp.cpp}) computes exact $P(x)$ for any T$+$CZ IQP
in $O(n2^{n/2})$ time and $2^{n/2}$ memory --- ground truth to
$n\!\approx\!62$ on a $36$\,GB machine, validated against dense
($6\times10^{-16}$) and against \texttt{record\_probabilities}
($6\times10^{-14}$ at $n{=}24,30$).
\end{itemize}
So for this family, \emph{everything exact costs $2^{n/2}$}, and hardness
claims must be framed against that scale. (Multiplicative approximation
remains GapP-hard for T-type IQP~\cite{bremner2016}; there is no poly-time
escape, but $n{=}72$ is exactly checkable at $\sim\!2^{36}$ work --- by us.)

\section{Implementation and validation}
A Python prototype (\texttt{research/chform\_backend}) is the reference; a
bit-packed C\texttt{++}20 port (\texttt{research/chform\_cpp}) is the
performance implementation. This revision also fixed a latent bug: the C++
amplitude took a \texttt{uint64} target and shifted by qubit index ---
undefined behavior for $n>64$ (the very frontier sizes previously reported,
where it happened to work only for the all-zeros target). Amplitudes are now
word-based (\texttt{amplitude\_words}), and the multi-word ($n>64$) paths are
covered by new tests.

\section{Benchmarks}
All contestants run single-threaded on an Apple M-series workstation ($36$\,GB;
\texttt{clifft} uses its scalar/NEON path --- an x86 AVX-512 host would favor
\texttt{clifft}); the MitM ground truth uses all cores but competes with
no one. Scripts and the raw JSON are committed.

\subsection{Extent, sparsification, free Cliffords}
As before (unchanged, re-verified): measured $L_1$ growth per $T$ is exactly
$2^{0.114}$; sparsification error tracks the bound to $\sim\!1\%$; the
single-shot estimator is unbiased. On the measured magic-conveyor the frame
composition performs \textbf{zero} per-term Clifford operations vs
$473$--$15{,}411$ for a measurement-aware pure stabilizer-rank simulator
($w{=}4$--$8$) --- the constant-factor advantage of the composition,
\emph{cf.}~\cite{bravyi2016,qassim2019} for its static prior art.

\subsection{The honest crossover}\label{sec:overlap}
Dense random IQP, $96$ uniform targets, exact ground truth by MitM
(cross-checked against \texttt{record\_probabilities} to $10^{-6}$ relative
everywhere both run); \texttt{clifft} baseline $=$ compile the measured
program (peak rank $n/2$) $+$ \texttt{record\_probabilities}. Backend at
budget $k=2^{0.228n}/\delta^2$, analytic normalization (\S\ref{sec:norm}),
timing includes build $+$ normalization $+$ all $96$ amplitude evaluations.
The error metric charges the full pipeline against the exact subset mass:
$\mathrm{TV}=\tfrac12\sum_x|\hat P(x)-P(x)|/\sum_x P(x)$. Means over 3
realizations ($n\le48$; 1 above), Table~\ref{tab:overlap} and
Fig.~\ref{fig:honest}:

The crossover is real but sits where the honest baseline puts it:
$n\!\approx\!34$ at $\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.17$, $n\!\approx\!48$ at
$\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.08$ --- not $n\!\approx\!22$. \texttt{clifft}'s exact
path grows as $2^{n/2}$ on the nose ($\times4.6$ per $+4$ qubits) and exits at
$n\!\approx\!58$--$62$ on memory; the backend's growth is $2^{0.228n}$
($\times1.9$ per $+4$).

\subsection{The accuracy dial}\label{sec:precision}
At $n{=}44$, $256$ targets, $4$ realizations, analytic normalization
(Fig.~\ref{fig:honest}, right): $\mathrm{TV}=0.144(4),\,0.101(3),\,0.0500(6),\,
0.0251(3)$ at $\delta=0.30,0.20,0.10,0.05$ --- i.e.\
$\mathrm{TV}=(0.50\pm0.01)\,\delta$, with runtime $\propto k\propto1/\delta^2$
($2.0\to73.9$\,s). The earlier draft's ``$\mathrm{TV}\approx0.47\,\delta$'' was
approximately right, \emph{but only because its metric excluded the norm
error}: re-running the same budgets with the $L{=}30$ estimated norm (the old
setting) degrades same-budget TV by up to $\sim\!2\times$ on unlucky draws
($0.07$--$0.32$ observed vs $0.07$--$0.21$ analytic), exactly the
$1.2/\sqrt{30}\approx22\%$ multiplicative noise of \S\ref{sec:norm}. The clean
law holds for the full pipeline only where normalization is analytic (unitary
product magic) or the norm budget is scaled up ($\chi L\sim1/\delta^4$).

\subsection{The frontier, honestly framed}\label{sec:frontier}
Dense IQP, $\delta{=}0.4$, single-shot build $+$ one amplitude
(\texttt{bench\_iqp.cpp}). The exact column is what \emph{any} known exact
method pays on this family ($2^{n/2}$: \texttt{clifft}-measured or MitM);
the old draft's ``$2^n$ / $64$\,ZB'' contrast overstated the gap by a factor
$2^{n/2}$.

Accuracy at the frontier: exact ground truth exists to $n\!\approx\!62$ (MitM),
where the measured TV still follows the dial ($0.086$ at $n{=}60$,
$\delta{=}0.15$). At $n{=}66$--$72$ \textbf{no exact check exists} (that is
the point); accuracy there rests on (i) the $\delta$-law holding at every
checkable size, (ii) the analytic normalization being exact for this family,
and (iii) the $n{>}64$ code paths now being tested ($W{=}2$ rows of
Table~\ref{tab:valid}) --- an extrapolation, stated as such, not a
measurement.

\subsection{qiskit-aer \texttt{extended\_stabilizer}}\label{sec:aer}
Now reproduced by a committed script (\texttt{bench\_aer.py}; aer $0.17.2$,
settings inline --- the old draft's numbers were unauditable). Sampling
(nn-IQP, 2000 shots, mixing $50$): \texttt{clifft} samples exactly at
$1.8$--$4.4\times10^6$ shots/s ($\mathrm{peak\_rank}=1$) vs aer's approximate
$2721\to44$ shots/s over $n=10\to28$ --- ratios $1630\times$ to
$40{,}000\times$. Strong simulation (dense IQP $n{=}24$, 96 uniform targets,
true $P\sim5.6\times10^{-8}$): \texttt{clifft} answers exactly in $3.5$\,ms;
aer's only route is shot frequency, and $30{,}000$ shots ($455$\,s) hit
$0/96$ targets ($\sim\!2\times10^7$ shots needed per expected hit). The
three-way split stands: \texttt{clifft} owns exact work while $2^{n/2}$ fits;
this backend owns approximate $P(x)$ beyond; \texttt{extended\_stabilizer}
(sampling-only, maintenance-frozen upstream) is dominated on both tasks.

\section{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Approximate}, with the guarantee of \S\ref{sec:guarantee}
(additive/typical, not per-$x$ relative), and \texttt{clifft}'s exactness
forfeited.
\item \textbf{The exact competition is $2^{n/2}$, not $2^n$}, on this family;
the backend's genuinely-unique regime starts near $n\!\approx\!62$, and its
speed advantage at moderate accuracy starts near $n\!\approx\!34$--$48$.
\item \textbf{Norm estimation} is the pipeline's accuracy-cost bottleneck for
generic circuits ($\chi L\sim1/\delta^4$); the clean results here lean on
analytic normalization, valid for unitary product magic only.
\item \textbf{The composition's unique value is still undemonstrated on a
natural workload.} The free-Clifford factor is real (op-counts) but
constant/poly with substantial static prior
art~\cite{bravyi2016,qassim2019,garcia2015,pashayan2022}; the defensible
novelty --- online frame $+$ dynamic measurement-driven collapse with
mid-circuit/adaptive measurement --- needs an adaptive-circuit benchmark
none of this note's IQP families exercises.
\item \textbf{Prototype gaps:} the Python engine's plain measurement path and
dedup materialize $2^n$ (validation-scale only); streaming sparsification is
implemented but untested/unbenchmarked; the C\texttt{++} engine has no
measurement path (build-and-query only).
\item External baselines (QuiZX, Quokka\#) not yet run; both do exact $P(x)$
at $t$ well beyond this note's $t{=}n$ and must appear in any publication
comparison.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
The validated machinery stands, and so does a real --- but honestly smaller
--- niche. Against \texttt{clifft}'s true exact fast path on dense IQP, the
CH-form backend wins from $n\!\approx\!34$ (coarse) / $n\!\approx\!48$
($\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.08$), and past $n\!\approx\!62$ it is the only
method of the three (dense block, forced replay, MitM) that runs at all:
$n{=}72$ in $267$\,s and $1.9$\,GB where anything exact needs
$\sim\!1$\,TB. The accuracy dial is clean and predictable
($\mathrm{TV}=0.50\,\delta$) once normalization is handled honestly. What
this note deliberately no longer claims: a crossover at $n\!\approx\!22$
(baseline artifact), $2^n$-scale frontier contrasts ($2^{n/2}$ is the honest
exact scale), sub-$10\%$ accuracy at budgets whose norm error exceeded that
(metric artifact), and novelty for free Cliffords as an idea (prior art). The
next experiments that would change the picture: an adaptive/mid-circuit
workload where the online composition is structurally unavailable to static
pipelines, and head-to-heads against QuiZX and Quokka\# on shared instances.
